The other guides are organized by concept. This one is organized by task: each
recipe opens with the report it builds and a local pipeline that builds it.
Variants, pitfalls and what changes on a database come after that output, the
longer ones under a sub-heading of their own, so you can stop at the first
sub-heading when the local answer is all you need. Read the recipes in any
order and skip the rest — no recipe uses a value another recipe defined, so
every one starts from
[`retail_sales`](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/retail_sales.html),
the package's 24-row example sales table, or from a small table it builds
itself.

Read [Get
started](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/get_started.html) first
if Grouping specifications are new to you. Each recipe links to the concept
guide that explains why its answer works.

## Installation

Install marginplyr from GitHub:

```{r}
#| eval: false

install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("sayuks/marginplyr")

# Used for the parts of this guide that execute against a database, for the
# crosstabs, and for the printed table.
install.packages(c("DBI", "duckdb", "knitr", "tidyr"))
```

```{r setup}
#| message: false

library(marginplyr)
library(dplyr)
```

Nothing beyond marginplyr's own dependencies is required. The chunks that run
against a database use DuckDB, the crosstabs reshape their result with tidyr,
and the printed table uses knitr, so those chunks evaluate only when the
package they need is installed at the version marginplyr asks for. Where a
package is missing or too old the code is still shown, but its output is
absent. Everything else runs either locally or
against `dbplyr::simulate_postgres()`, which needs no database and no optional
package.

```{r}
#| include: false

# Base R translates its own diagnostics, and a rejected call shows them, so
# the page carries English whatever locale it is rendered in.
Sys.setenv(LANGUAGE = "en")

# `marginplyr_suggest_available()` answers what a bare installation check
# could not: whether the installed package satisfies the version DESCRIPTION
# requires. AGENTS.md is authoritative for which guards must go through it.
source(system.file("suggests", "guard.R", package = "marginplyr"))

has_duckdb <- marginplyr_suggest_available("DBI") &&
  marginplyr_suggest_available("duckdb")
has_tidyr <- marginplyr_suggest_available("tidyr")
has_knitr <- marginplyr_suggest_available("knitr")
```

## Put each subtotal with the rows it summarizes

By default a Margin result promises no particular arrangement, so subtotals
can land anywhere:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .by = year,
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  )
```

`.sort = "last"` asks for a Margin order instead. Within each fixed `.by` key
every dimension contributes its Grouping bit — the `0`/`1` flag
`grouping_bit()` returns for it, `1` where aggregation removed it — before its
own value, so each subtotal sits directly beneath the rows it summarizes:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .by = year,
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

`"first"` puts each subtotal above its rows instead, as [Put the totals above
the rows they summarize](#put-the-totals-above-the-rows-they-summarize) shows.
The label's text never decides where a subtotal goes, so changing it moves
nothing, and neither does the locale; whether there is a label does decide how
a non-factor dimension sorts, as [Keep a numeric dimension in numeric
order](#keep-a-numeric-dimension-in-numeric-order) shows. Within a level, rows
sort ascending by value. The `NA` store sorts after the named stores but
still ahead of the region subtotal: each dimension contributes its Grouping
bit before its missingness, so a margin outranks a missing value rather than
competing with one.

**A Margin order belongs to the object the verb returned, not to anything
derived from it.** Any later verb is free to reorder, and on a lazy backend
one usually does — see [The same join against a lazy
table](#the-same-join-against-a-lazy-table) for a join that drops it, and the
warning dbplyr gives when it does.
When some other presentation order is what you want, write the key yourself as
an `arrange()` you control: [Sort the newest year
first](#sort-the-newest-year-first) reverses one dimension, and [Sort regions
and stores by revenue](#sort-regions-and-stores-by-revenue) orders by a
measure.

[Grouping
identity](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/grouping_identity.html)
explains why Grouping-plan order and a Margin order answer different
questions.

### Keep a numeric dimension in numeric order

A non-missing `.margin_label` turns the dimension into character, and the
Margin order sorts the values the result holds, so a numeric dimension comes
back in text order:

```{r}
months <- tibble(month = c(2L, 9L, 10L), revenue = c(100, 200, 300))

months |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(month),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

`"10"` sorts before `"2"`. Make the column a factor first, which keeps its
levels in numeric order and adds the label as a last level:

```{r}
months |>
  mutate(month = factor(month)) |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(month),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

Or keep the column numeric with `.margin_label = NULL`, which shows each
margin as `NA` instead of a label:

```{r}
months |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(month),
    .margin_label = NULL,
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

## Put the totals above the rows they summarize

A report that reads top-down — the grand total first, then each region's
subtotal ahead of its stores — is `.sort = "first"`. It is the same Margin
order as `"last"` with every Grouping bit sorted the other way, so each
subtotal sits directly above the rows it summarizes:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .sort = "first"
  )
```

### Put the grand total on top and subtotals under their rows

No `.sort` value mixes the two placements. Write the key as an `arrange()`
instead: retain the Grouping bits, sort the region's bit descending so the
grand total comes first, and the store's bit ascending so each region's
subtotal comes after its stores. Each value follows its bit, missing values
last, as in the Margin order:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    rb = grouping_bit(region),
    sb = grouping_bit(store),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(rb), is.na(region), region, sb, is.na(store), store) |>
  select(-rb, -sb)
```

[Sort the newest year first](#sort-the-newest-year-first) writes the same kind
of key with one value reversed.

## Sort the newest year first

`.sort = "last"` lists every dimension's values in ascending order, so 2025
comes before 2026. To put the newest year at the top and keep each subtotal
under its own rows, write that order out as an `arrange()` and reverse one
term. The order takes each dimension in turn and sorts on its Grouping bit —
the `0`/`1` flag `grouping_bit()` returns, `1` where aggregation removed the
dimension — then on whether its value is missing, then on the value. Retain
the bits in the summary, and put `desc()` on the year's value:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    yb = grouping_bit(year),
    rb = grouping_bit(region),
    .grouping = rollup(year, region)
  ) |>
  arrange(yb, is.na(year), desc(year), rb, is.na(region), region) |>
  select(-yb, -rb)
```

2026 sits above 2025 and each subtotal is still under its own rows, because
everything ahead of the reversed term is what it was. `desc(year)` gets the
years right only because the label has made `year` text and every year has
four digits; for a numeric dimension whose values differ in length, give the
key a factor or use `.margin_label = NULL`, as in [Keep a numeric dimension in
numeric order](#keep-a-numeric-dimension-in-numeric-order).

*Margin order* in the [`margin_verbs`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/margin_verbs.html#margin-order)
states the whole key.

### Sort a lazy table the same way

The Grouping bits of a `rollup()` are computed in the query underneath the one
the ordering sits in, so dropping them with `select()` keeps the order, and the
pipeline runs on a database unchanged. It writes `na.rm = TRUE` in both places
so that the results match: locally a missing measure makes every subtotal and
total that includes it `NA`, while a SQL aggregate always drops missing
values, and dbplyr warns when `na.rm = TRUE` is absent:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

# `shared_home = FALSE` keeps DuckDB's extension cache and stored secrets in
# the session's temporary directory rather than in `~/.duckdb`.
con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(shared_home = FALSE))
duckdb_sales <- dplyr::copy_to(con, retail_sales, "retail_sales")

duckdb_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    yb = grouping_bit(year),
    rb = grouping_bit(region),
    .grouping = rollup(year, region)
  ) |>
  arrange(yb, is.na(year), desc(year), rb, is.na(region), region) |>
  select(-yb, -rb) |>
  collect()
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

## Sort regions and stores by revenue

A report that lists the largest region first, and the largest store first
within each region, orders on a number no column holds yet: each region's
revenue, on every one of its rows. That number is already in the result as the
region's subtotal row, so a grouped `mutate()` can copy it onto the region's
rows before the `arrange()`. `rb` and `sb` are the region's and the store's
Grouping bits — the `0`/`1` flag `grouping_bit()` returns, `1` where
aggregation removed the dimension — and the `sb` term keeps each subtotal
under its own stores:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    rb = grouping_bit(region),
    sb = grouping_bit(store),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    .by = c(rb, region),
    region_revenue = max(ifelse(sb == 1, revenue, NA), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(rb, desc(region_revenue), region, sb, desc(revenue), store) |>
  select(region, store, revenue)
```

The `mutate()` groups by `rb` as well as `region` because a displayed value
does not say which grouping set a row came from. With `.margin_label = NULL`,
the grand-total row and the rows whose region is missing in the source both
show `NA`. Grouped on `region` alone they share one group, and the region
with no name is ranked by the grand total. A source region equal to the label
meets the grand-total row the same way. Keying on the Grouping bit and the
value together is the rule [Show each row as a percent of a level further
up](#show-each-row-as-a-percent-of-a-level-further-up) states for a join key.

A fixed `.by` key on the verb belongs in both steps. Add `year` to the
`mutate()`'s `.by`, so that each year's regions are ranked by that year's
subtotal, and put `year` first in the `arrange()`, so that the years do not
interleave:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    rb = grouping_bit(region),
    sb = grouping_bit(store),
    .by = year,
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    .by = c(year, rb, region),
    region_revenue = max(ifelse(sb == 1, revenue, NA), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(year, rb, desc(region_revenue), region, sb, desc(revenue), store) |>
  select(year, region, store, revenue)
```

A deeper rollup needs one such helper per level that is ordered by a measure.
For example, in `rollup(region, store, product)`, ranking stores within their
region needs a store-level helper keyed on `rb`, `region`, `sb` and `store`.

### Keep the helper column on a lazy table

On a lazy backend, dropping a helper column can cost the order. Whether it
does is decided by the query dbplyr builds, which this package does not own —
but you are told when it happens, either by dbplyr warning that it discarded
an `ORDER BY` or by the database refusing a query that orders on a column no
longer in it.

A Grouping bit can be dropped, because it is computed in the query underneath
the one the ordering sits in. `region_revenue` cannot: you computed it after
the summary, so it is in the same query as the ordering, and dropping it
leaves an `ORDER BY` naming a column that is gone:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(shared_home = FALSE))
duckdb_sales <- dplyr::copy_to(con, retail_sales, "retail_sales")
```

```{r}
#| label: dropping-a-computed-sort-term
#| error: true
#| purl: false
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

duckdb_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    rb = grouping_bit(region),
    sb = grouping_bit(store),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    .by = c(rb, region),
    region_revenue = max(ifelse(sb == 1, revenue, NA), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(rb, desc(region_revenue), region, sb, desc(revenue), store) |>
  select(region, store, revenue) |>
  collect()
```

Keep the column and the result stays lazy and stays ordered, at the cost of
carrying it:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

duckdb_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    rb = grouping_bit(region),
    sb = grouping_bit(store),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    .by = c(rb, region),
    region_revenue = max(ifelse(sb == 1, revenue, NA), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(rb, desc(region_revenue), region, sb, desc(revenue), store) |>
  collect()
```

`collect()` before the `select()` is the other way, and gives up laziness to
get a report with no helper columns in it.

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

## Show the top stores in each region with full totals

A report that lists each region's two largest stores still owes the reader
each region's whole revenue in its subtotal. Summarize first, then rank the
detail rows within each region and keep the top ones together with every
margin row. `rb` and `sb` are the region's and the store's Grouping bits, and
`min_rank()` gives the margin rows no rank:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    rb = grouping_bit(region),
    sb = grouping_bit(store),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    .by = c(rb, region),
    store_rank = min_rank(desc(ifelse(sb == 0L, revenue, NA)))
  ) |>
  filter(sb == 1L | store_rank <= 2L) |>
  select(region, store, revenue, store_rank)
```

East's subtotal is still 41900, although its unnamed store is not listed.
Keeping only the top stores *before* the summary is the mistake to avoid: the
dropped store then leaves every total that includes it, and East's subtotal
and the grand total shrink to the stores shown. The `mutate()` groups by `rb`
as well as `region` for the reason [Sort regions and stores by
revenue](#sort-regions-and-stores-by-revenue) gives.

## Report by year, quarter and month

A calendar hierarchy is a `rollup()` over date parts, and the parts are
ordinary columns: derive them with `mutate()` before the summary. Make the
month a factor with the calendar's levels, because the Margin order sorts the
values the result holds and month names sort alphabetically, Feb before Jan:

```{r}
orders <- tibble(
  date = as.Date(c(
    "2025-01-15", "2025-02-03", "2025-11-20",
    "2026-01-08", "2026-04-30", "2026-05-12"
  )),
  revenue = c(120, 80, 200, 150, 90, 60)
)

orders |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(format(date, "%Y")),
    quarter = quarters(date),
    month = factor(
      month.abb[as.integer(format(date, "%m"))],
      levels = month.abb
    )
  ) |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(year, quarter, month),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

`month.abb` and `quarters()` give the same names in every locale, where
`months()` and `format(date, "%b")` follow the session's language. The quarters
need no factor, since `"Q1"` to `"Q4"` already sort in calendar order. [Keep
a numeric dimension in numeric
order](#keep-a-numeric-dimension-in-numeric-order) explains why the label
turns `year` into text.

## Make a crosstab (pivot table) with totals on both edges

A crosstab, or pivot table, puts one dimension down the side, another across
the top, and a total on both edges: products as rows, stores as columns, a `Total`
column on the right and a `Total` row at the bottom. `cube()` produces every
cell of that table, including both sets of totals and their corner,
`tidyr::pivot_wider()` lays it out, and `relocate()` puts the `Total` column
last:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_tidyr

retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = cube(product, store),
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = store, values_from = revenue) |>
  relocate(Total, .after = last_col())
```

**The row order does not place the columns.** `pivot_wider()` creates a
column for each store in the order it first meets that store in the rows.
`.sort = "last"` puts the `Total` row at the bottom, but the first product's
rows name only the stores that sold it, so without the `relocate()` the
`Total` column lands after those stores, ahead of the rest.

Two kinds of empty cell come out of the pivot. A store that is missing in the
source becomes a column named `NA`, beside the named stores. A product and
store with no rows between them is `NA` in the wide table, because there is
no summary row for that cell; pass `values_fill = 0` to `pivot_wider()` when
such a cell should read as zero revenue.

### Pivot a lazy result after collecting

On a lazy table `pivot_wider()` builds the wide
table in SQL. That query reads the sorted summary as a subquery, so dbplyr
drops the Margin order and warns, as in [The same join against a lazy
table](#the-same-join-against-a-lazy-table). The columns and rows then come in
whatever order the database produces them, so neither `Total` has to land on
its edge:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb && has_tidyr

con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(shared_home = FALSE))
duckdb_sales <- dplyr::copy_to(con, retail_sales, "retail_sales")

duckdb_crosstab <- duckdb_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    .grouping = cube(product, store),
    .sort = "last"
  )

duckdb_crosstab |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = store, values_from = revenue) |>
  collect()
```

The summary is one row per cell, so collecting it first costs little, and the
local pivot then reads the rows in Margin order:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb && has_tidyr

duckdb_crosstab |>
  collect() |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = store, values_from = revenue) |>
  relocate(Total, .after = last_col())
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb && has_tidyr

DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

## Show each crosstab cell as a percent of its row or column

A crosstab of percents — each product's revenue split across channels, with
the totals still on both edges — divides every cell by its row's `Total`. The
share helpers do not reach it: `share_of_parent()` refuses a `cube()`, which
has no single parent level, and `share_of_total()` with `.by = product` gives
the row percents but has no all-products row to show. Retain both Grouping
bits instead, and divide each cell by the cell of its row whose channel bit is
one — grouped by the product's bit and value, for the reason [Sort regions and
stores by revenue](#sort-regions-and-stores-by-revenue) gives:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_tidyr

retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    pb = grouping_bit(product),
    cb = grouping_bit(channel),
    .grouping = cube(product, channel),
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    .by = c(pb, product),
    pct_of_row = round(100 * revenue / revenue[cb == 1L], 1)
  ) |>
  select(product, channel, pct_of_row) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = channel, values_from = pct_of_row) |>
  relocate(Total, .after = last_col())
```

Every row reads 100 in its `Total` column, and the `Total` row splits all
revenue across channels. For percents of each column, swap the roles: group by
the channel's bit and value, and divide by the row whose product bit is one:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_tidyr

retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    pb = grouping_bit(product),
    cb = grouping_bit(channel),
    .grouping = cube(product, channel),
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    .by = c(cb, channel),
    pct_of_column = round(100 * revenue / revenue[pb == 1L], 1)
  ) |>
  select(product, channel, pct_of_column) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = channel, values_from = pct_of_column) |>
  relocate(Total, .after = last_col())
```

## Show each row as a percent of the total

A percent-of-total column divides each row by a total, and the report decides
which one: each year's own total, or the whole table's. `share_of_total()`
divides a summary by the same summary on the Grand total set and returns the
fraction; multiply it by 100 for a percent. Which rows that set covers is
decided by the fixed `.by` keys, and that is the whole of the choice. With
`.by = year`, each year is its own denominator:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    share_of_year = share_of_total(revenue),
    .by = year,
    .grouping = rollup(region),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

The region rows inside each year add up to one, and 2025 contributes nothing
to 2026's denominator. The year's own row is the denominator, so its share is
one by definition rather than by addition. Move the dimension out of `.by` and
into the Grouping specification, and the same helper measures against the
whole table instead:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    share_overall = share_of_total(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(year, region),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

Now every row is a share of all four region-years together, and the year rows
are subtotals rather than partitions. Both calls are correct; they answer
different questions, and `.by` is what distinguishes them.

**On SQLite and on a simulated connection, either call is refused until it sets
`.check_share_source = FALSE`.** marginplyr establishes that a share's source
is a number by asking the dialect, and SQLite answers `sum()` of text with a
number while a simulator executes nothing to ask. [Parent shares use a staged
lazy
query](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/database_backends.html#parent-shares-use-a-staged-lazy-query)
states the rule; DuckDB runs both calls unchanged.

For a denominator one rollup level up rather than at the top, use
`share_of_parent()`. The
[`share_of_parent()`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/share_of_parent.html)
documents both helpers, and [Compare a summary with the
whole](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/get_started.html#compare-a-summary-with-the-whole)
compares them side by side. For a level between the two, [Show each row as a
percent of a level further
up](#show-each-row-as-a-percent-of-a-level-further-up) runs the same `.by`
lever the other way.

## Show each row as a percent of a level further up

In a three-level report an ordinary question sits between the parent and the
top: what fraction of its *region* is a channel row? `share_of_parent()`
divides by the level immediately above and `share_of_total()` by the top. A
store's parent is its region, but a channel's is its store, so neither helper
answers it as written.

Move the ancestor dimension into `.by`. The Grand total set of a fixed
partition is that partition's own total, so `share_of_total()` measures
against the region with no join and no key of your own:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    share_of_region = share_of_total(revenue),
    .by = region,
    .grouping = rollup(store, channel),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

Placement is what chooses a denominator, and this is the lever from [Show each
row as a percent of the total](#show-each-row-as-a-percent-of-the-total) run
the other way: move a column out of `.by` to pool partitions, move it in to
measure against it.

What the move costs is the levels above the ancestor. `region` is a fixed key,
so no grouping set of the plan pools regions and the result has no all-regions
row. When a report needs both — a share against an ancestor level *and* the
levels above it — read the ancestor level out of the result and join it back.

The example below measures against the store level rather than the region,
because `store` is the dimension with a missing source value, and the join key
has to tell that value apart from a margin. It adds `product` so that the
store is not the channel row's parent, which `share_of_parent()` would
already answer: in `rollup(region, store, product, channel)` the parent of a
channel row is its product, and the store level `(region, store)` is two
levels further up. Select that level and keep the revenue under a name of its
own:

```{r}
store_totals <- retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    store_revenue = sum(revenue),
    region_absent = grouping_bit(region),
    store_absent = grouping_bit(store),
    product_absent = grouping_bit(product),
    channel_absent = grouping_bit(channel),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store, product, channel)
  ) |>
  filter(
    region_absent == 0L,
    store_absent == 0L,
    product_absent == 1L,
    channel_absent == 1L
  ) |>
  select(region, region_absent, store, store_absent, store_revenue)

store_totals
```

Then summarize the whole rollup, retain the same bits, and divide. The
division is ordinary R, so a zero denominator gives `NaN` where the share
helpers give `NA`:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    region_absent = grouping_bit(region),
    store_absent = grouping_bit(store),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store, product, channel),
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    store_totals,
    by = c("region", "region_absent", "store", "store_absent"),
    na_matches = "na"
  ) |>
  mutate(share_of_store = revenue / store_revenue) |>
  select(region, store, product, channel, revenue, share_of_store)
```

The store with no name gets its own denominator, and the two levels that have
no store — the region subtotals and the grand total — get `NA` rather than a
number.

The share helpers take no argument naming an ancestor level, so this join is
how a report reaches one together with the levels above it. Two things make
the join come out right, and neither announces itself: the Grouping bits in
its key, and `na_matches = "na"` on a database.

### Key the join on Grouping identity

The level is
selected by `grouping_bit()` rather than by a Margin label, for the reason
[Show only the subtotals, only the detail, or one
level](#show-only-the-subtotals-only-the-detail-or-one-level)
gives: a source
value can equal the label. The same argument reaches the join key, which is
why each dimension's bit travels beside its value. Without the bits, a row
whose store is *omitted* joins to the row whose store is *missing in the
source*, because both display the same thing. With `.margin_label = NULL` they
are both `NA` and the result is a number rather than a gap:

```{r}
label_free_totals <- retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    store_revenue = sum(revenue),
    region_absent = grouping_bit(region),
    store_absent = grouping_bit(store),
    product_absent = grouping_bit(product),
    channel_absent = grouping_bit(channel),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store, product, channel),
    .margin_label = NULL
  ) |>
  filter(
    region_absent == 0L,
    store_absent == 0L,
    product_absent == 1L,
    channel_absent == 1L
  ) |>
  select(region, store, store_revenue)

retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store, product, channel),
    .margin_label = NULL,
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  left_join(label_free_totals, by = c("region", "store"), na_matches = "na") |>
  mutate(share_of_store = revenue / store_revenue) |>
  filter(region == "East", is.na(store)) |>
  select(region, store, product, channel, revenue, share_of_store)
```

The last row is East's region subtotal, and its share is greater than one: it
took the unnamed store's revenue as its denominator. [Grouping
identity](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/grouping_identity.html#three-kinds-of-apparent-missingness)
sets out the three kinds of apparent missingness this confuses, and why
`share_of_parent()` cannot make the same mistake internally.

### The join on a database

`na_matches = "na"` is written explicitly because the default differs by
backend. `dplyr::left_join()` matches `NA` to `NA`, so a local pipeline is
right without the argument. dbplyr's method does not. The same pipeline
therefore drops the unnamed store's share against a database, and nothing
reports that it did. Both halves are below — the join as written, then the
same join with the argument dropped:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(shared_home = FALSE))
duckdb_sales <- dplyr::copy_to(con, retail_sales, "retail_sales")

duckdb_store_totals <- duckdb_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    store_revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    region_absent = grouping_bit(region),
    store_absent = grouping_bit(store),
    product_absent = grouping_bit(product),
    channel_absent = grouping_bit(channel),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store, product, channel)
  ) |>
  filter(
    region_absent == 0L,
    store_absent == 0L,
    product_absent == 1L,
    channel_absent == 1L
  ) |>
  select(region, region_absent, store, store_absent, store_revenue)

duckdb_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    region_absent = grouping_bit(region),
    store_absent = grouping_bit(store),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store, product, channel)
  ) |>
  left_join(
    duckdb_store_totals,
    by = c("region", "region_absent", "store", "store_absent"),
    na_matches = "na"
  ) |>
  mutate(share_of_store = revenue / store_revenue) |>
  filter(is.na(store)) |>
  select(region, store, product, channel, revenue, share_of_store) |>
  collect()
```

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

duckdb_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    region_absent = grouping_bit(region),
    store_absent = grouping_bit(store),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store, product, channel)
  ) |>
  left_join(
    duckdb_store_totals,
    by = c("region", "region_absent", "store", "store_absent")
  ) |>
  mutate(share_of_store = revenue / store_revenue) |>
  filter(is.na(store)) |>
  select(region, store, product, channel, revenue, share_of_store) |>
  collect()
```

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

The unnamed store keeps its share in the first and loses it in the second, and
the two calls differ by one argument. Neither DuckDB summary asks for `.sort`:
as [The same join against a lazy
table](#the-same-join-against-a-lazy-table) shows, dbplyr drops a Margin order
a join reads, so `arrange()` after the join, or collect first.

## Show only the subtotals, only the detail, or one level

A report that shows only the region subtotals of a cube — every region, with
the channels pooled — keeps the rows of that one grouping set; [Keep every
margin, only the detail, or one
depth](#keep-every-margin-only-the-detail-or-one-depth) keeps several. Filter on
Grouping identity
rather than on a Margin label: a source value can equal the label, and the
label can be changed or set to `NULL`. The obstacle is knowing which value to
ask for — and guessing the bit order is easy to get backwards.

Do not guess. `inspect_grouping()` prints the answer for every set in the plan
before any data is summarized. Selecting the two columns read below prints
them in full:

```{r}
inspect_grouping(
  .data = retail_sales,
  .grouping = cube(region, channel)
) |>
  select(grouping_bits, grouping_id)
```

Read `grouping_bits` beside `grouping_id`: the last dimension is the least
significant bit, so `channel` alone being omitted is `1`, `region` alone is
`2`, and both is `3`. Retain the identifier in the summary and filter on it:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    absence = grouping_id(region, channel),
    .grouping = cube(region, channel),
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  filter(absence == 1L)
```

`grouping_id()` can also be written with no columns at all, which the
[`grouping_bit()`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/grouping_bit.html) defines
against the resolved plan. It is the same identifier here, and there is no
second list of dimensions to keep in step with the specification:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    absence = grouping_id(),
    .grouping = cube(region, channel),
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  filter(absence == 1L)
```

Two steps are required because `grouping_id()` and `grouping_bit()` are
contextual summary helpers. They read the grouping set that produced a row,
which only the summary knows, so calling one inside `filter()` is rejected:

```{r}
#| label: grouping-bit-in-filter
#| error: true
#| purl: false

retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = cube(region, channel)
  ) |>
  filter(grouping_bit(channel) == 1L)
```

For a single dimension, `grouping_bit()` avoids the bit arithmetic altogether:
retain one flag column per dimension and filter on the flags. The
[`grouping_bit()`
reference](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/grouping_bit.html) compares
all four identity values and states their duplicate-occurrence rules, and the
[Grouping identity
guide](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/grouping_identity.html)
works through what that comparison means in practice.

### Keep every margin, only the detail, or one depth

The Grouping identifier is `0` on the detail rows and positive on every
margin, so one comparison keeps either side. `grouping_id() > 0` keeps every
subtotal and the grand total:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    absence = grouping_id(),
    .grouping = cube(region, channel),
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  filter(absence > 0L)
```

`filter(absence == 0L)` keeps the detail alone.

A depth — every two-way subtotal of a three-way cube, say — is the sets that
omit one dimension each. The sum of the Grouping bits counts the dimensions a
row omits:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    rb = grouping_bit(region),
    pb = grouping_bit(product),
    cb = grouping_bit(channel),
    .grouping = cube(region, product, channel),
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  filter(rb + pb + cb == 1L) |>
  select(-rb, -pb, -cb)
```

The plan answers the same question without a bit column per dimension: in its
`.format = "list"` form, `lengths(omitted)` counts each set's omitted
dimensions, and `.id` carries the set onto the result:

```{r}
two_way_sets <- retail_sales |>
  inspect_grouping(
    .grouping = cube(region, product, channel),
    .format = "list"
  ) |>
  filter(lengths(omitted) == 1L) |>
  pull(set_id)

retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .grouping = cube(region, product, channel),
    .id = "set",
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  filter(set %in% two_way_sets)
```

## Add a level column: detail, subtotal or total

A report often needs a column saying what each row is — store detail, a region
subtotal, or the all-regions total — so that a reader, a later `filter()` or a
table's styling can tell them apart. `.id` numbers the grouping-set occurrence
behind each row, and `inspect_grouping()` returns one row per occurrence keyed
by the same number. Joining them attaches whatever name you care to write.

Build the name on the plan first. `inspect_grouping()` returns an ordinary
tibble with no custom class, so ordinary dplyr applies, and cutting it down to
two columns keeps the plan's five description columns out of the report:

```{r}
sales_levels <- retail_sales |>
  inspect_grouping(
    .by = year,
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    level = case_when(
      omitted == "()" ~ "Store detail",
      omitted == "(store)" ~ "Region subtotal",
      .default = "All regions"
    )
  ) |>
  select(set_id, level)

sales_levels
```

Then join it onto the result:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .by = year,
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .id = "set",
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  left_join(sales_levels, by = c(set = "set_id"))
```

### The same join against a lazy table

`inspect_grouping()` is local even when `.data` is not: it reads captured
column metadata and the Grouping plan, never the source rows. A lazy result
and a local tibble have no common source, so dbplyr refuses the join
outright, and its message names the two `copy` routes out of the refusal:

```{r}
postgres_sales <- dbplyr::tbl_lazy(
  retail_sales,
  con = dbplyr::simulate_postgres()
)

postgres_report <- postgres_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = year,
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .id = "set",
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: join-without-copy
#| error: true
#| purl: false

postgres_report |>
  left_join(sales_levels, by = c(set = "set_id"))
```

`copy = "inline"` compiles the plan into the query as a `VALUES` list, which
suits a table holding one row per grouping set and needs no permission to
write one:

```{r}
postgres_report |>
  left_join(sales_levels, by = c(set = "set_id"), copy = "inline")
```

Two conditions come with that route.

**The Margin order does not survive the join.** As [Put each subtotal with the
rows it summarizes](#put-each-subtotal-with-the-rows-it-summarizes) put it, a
Margin order is a property of the object the verb returned, not of anything
derived from it. Here dbplyr removes it: the joined query reads the sorted
summary as a subquery, and dbplyr leaves out an `ORDER BY` in a subquery that
has no `LIMIT` — the warning printed under the inline join above is dbplyr
saying so. Run against a live database, the rows come back in whatever
order the database produces:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(shared_home = FALSE))
duckdb_sales <- dplyr::copy_to(con, retail_sales, "retail_sales")

duckdb_report <- duckdb_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = year,
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .id = "set",
    .sort = "last"
  )

duckdb_report |>
  left_join(sales_levels, by = c(set = "set_id"), copy = "inline") |>
  collect()
```

The subtotals are scattered and the years interleave. The signal is dbplyr's
warning, *ORDER BY is ignored in subqueries without LIMIT*: it names nothing in
marginplyr, but it is raised whenever the query is rendered, so `show_query()` and
`collect()` both give it. `.sort` is an argument of the Margin verb, so it
cannot be applied again afterwards. Leave it off a lazy summary you are about
to join, and order with `arrange()` after the join, or collect first as below.

**The plan has to be in the default `.format = "text"`.** The list columns of
`.format = "list"` have no SQL type, and the failure surfaces while dbplyr
renders the query, without naming `.format`. The same `ORDER BY` warning comes
first, because `postgres_report` is sorted:

```{r}
list_levels <- inspect_grouping(
  .data = postgres_sales,
  .by = year,
  .grouping = rollup(region, store),
  .format = "list"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: join-list-format
#| error: true
#| purl: false

postgres_report |>
  left_join(list_levels, by = c(set = "set_id"), copy = "inline") |>
  show_query()
```

Prefer `collect()` before the join whenever the result is a report you are
about to read. It is the same shape as the local join at the top of this
recipe: the plan is one row per grouping set and a finished summary is already
small, so nothing is gained by making the database perform the join — and
collecting first keeps the Margin order, allows `.format = "list"`, and needs
no `copy` argument at all:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

duckdb_report |>
  collect() |>
  left_join(sales_levels, by = c(set = "set_id"))
```

Same query, same plan, same join — and every subtotal is back under the rows
it summarizes.

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

[Database and lazy
backends](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/database_backends.html)
covers query shape and execution for lazy inputs generally.

## Style the total rows in a printed table

A table package styles rows by a column it can test, and a Grouping bit is
that column: `1` on every row where aggregation removed its dimension, whatever
the label reads. Retain it, use it to style the rows — here by setting them in bold in
`knitr::kable()`'s Markdown — and drop it before printing:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_knitr

retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    sb = grouping_bit(store),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(region, store, revenue),
      function(x) ifelse(sb == 1L, paste0("**", x, "**"), x)
    )
  ) |>
  select(-sb) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

`sb` is `1` on the region subtotals and on the grand total, since the store is
omitted from both. A package with its own row styling takes the same column in
place of the `mutate()`; [Add a level column: detail, subtotal or
total](#add-a-level-column-detail-subtotal-or-total) names the levels when one
style per level is wanted.

## Report a mean, a median or a distinct count

Measures that cannot be added up — an average sale, a median, a count of
distinct values — are written as ordinary summary expressions:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    avg_sale = mean(revenue),
    median_units = median(units),
    channels = n_distinct(channel),
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

Each level is computed from the source rows, not from the rows below it:
West's average sale is taken over its twelve sales rather than its two stores'
averages, and East's two channels are counted once rather than summed across
its three stores.

## Report a weighted mean

`weighted.mean()` works on a data frame, but not on every backend: dbplyr
passes it to the database as written, which DuckDB rejects with a binder
error, and marginplyr refuses it on an Arrow input when Arrow's engine cannot
evaluate it. Written as two sums the same measure runs on a data frame,
DuckDB, Arrow and dtplyr alike. Here the average price per unit sold, against
the plain mean of the prices:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  mutate(price = revenue / units) |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    mean_price = mean(price),
    avg_price = sum(price * units) / sum(units),
    .grouping = rollup(region),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

[Other lazy
backends](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/database_backends.html#other-lazy-backends)
in Database and lazy backends shows the Arrow refusal.

## Fix a nested-aggregate error on a database

An ordinary mean, median or distinct count needs none of what follows; see
[Report a mean, a median or a distinct
count](#report-a-mean-a-median-or-a-distinct-count). A calculation that compares each row with an aggregate of its own group — here,
the share of revenue coming from rows above their own set's mean — works on a
local data frame and fails on a database with a nested-aggregate error. On a
local data frame dplyr hands the summary expression the whole group, so it
works directly:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    above_mean_share =
      sum(revenue[revenue > mean(revenue, na.rm = TRUE)], na.rm = TRUE) /
      sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = year,
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

Against a database the same expression has to compile to SQL aggregates, and
this one does not: the comparison needs an average that is itself an aggregate
over the same group, which no dialect allows inside another aggregate. The
error comes from the database, with its own wording:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(shared_home = FALSE))
duckdb_sales <- dplyr::copy_to(con, retail_sales, "retail_sales")
```

```{r}
#| label: nested-aggregate
#| error: true
#| purl: false
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

duckdb_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    above_mean_share =
      sum(revenue[revenue > mean(revenue, na.rm = TRUE)], na.rm = TRUE) /
      sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = year,
    .grouping = rollup(region, store)
  ) |>
  collect()
```

`expand_with_margins()` is the way through. It emits one copy of each source
row for every grouping set, which turns the one summary pass into ordinary
rows you can take as many passes over as the calculation needs — a window
function for the group's mean, then an aggregate over the comparison. It stays
lazy throughout:

```{r}
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

duckdb_sales |>
  expand_with_margins(
    .by = year,
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .id = "set"
  ) |>
  group_by(year, region, store, set) |>
  mutate(set_mean = mean(revenue, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  summarize(
    above_mean_share =
      sum(ifelse(revenue > set_mean, revenue, 0), na.rm = TRUE) /
      sum(revenue, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  collect()
```

`set` is in the `group_by()` because the dimensions alone do not identify a
grouping set. Under `.margin_label = NULL`, a store that is missing in the
source and the region's store margin both show `NA`, and without `set` their
copies would merge into one group.

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: !expr has_duckdb

DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

Every value matches the local calculation above. The two tables are not laid
out alike — this one carries the `set` column and is in no Margin order,
because the pipeline ends in an ordinary `summarize()` rather than in a Margin
verb — so compare them by key rather than row by row. `expand_with_margins()`
takes `.sort` itself, which orders the expansion rather than what follows it:

```{r}
retail_sales |>
  filter(year == 2026L, month == "Jan") |>
  expand_with_margins(
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .id = "set",
    .sort = "last"
  ) |>
  select(set, region, store, units)
```

Each region's detail copies now sit above its margin copies, and the
all-regions copies come last. Without `.sort` the expansion promises no row
order.

The cost is in the row count: expansion produces one copy of the input per
grouping set, so a plan with many sets multiplies the rows every later step
processes. On some backends each copy also reads the input again; the guide
below says which. Reach for this when the
aggregation pass genuinely cannot express the calculation, not to avoid
writing a summary.

[Database and lazy
backends](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/vignettes/database_backends.html)
shows the SQL `expand_with_margins()` generates, which is the portable
`UNION ALL` form on every backend.

## Call a Margin verb from your own function

A function such as `report(data, ...)` hands its caller's grouping columns, a
measure and a fixed key to a Margin verb the way it would hand them to
`dplyr::summarize()`. Every route below produces exactly what the direct call
produces:

```{r}
direct <- retail_sales |>
  summarize_with_margins(
    revenue = sum(revenue),
    .by = year,
    .grouping = rollup(region, store),
    .sort = "last"
  )
```

Column names held as strings go through `all_of()` wherever the verb selects
columns, inside a Grouping specification or in `.by`, and through
`.data[[ ]]` inside a summary expression:

```{r}
report_by_name <- function(data, dims, by, measure) {
  data |>
    summarize_with_margins(
      revenue = sum(.data[[measure]]),
      .by = all_of(by),
      .grouping = rollup(all_of(dims)),
      .sort = "last"
    )
}

report_by_name(retail_sales, c("region", "store"), "year", "revenue") |>
  identical(direct)
```

A bare vector, `rollup(dims)`, selects the same columns but draws a
deprecation warning from tidyselect for an external vector; `all_of()` is the
spelling that does not.

Dots forwarded into a specification constructor take what the caller wrote,
bare names or strings:

```{r}
report_by_dots <- function(data, ...) {
  data |>
    summarize_with_margins(
      revenue = sum(.data$revenue),
      .by = "year",
      .grouping = rollup(...),
      .sort = "last"
    )
}

report_by_dots(retail_sales, region, store) |>
  identical(direct)
report_by_dots(retail_sales, "region", "store") |>
  identical(direct)
```

Embracing an argument with `{{ }}` forwards one bare column or name anywhere
the verb takes one: a specification, `.by`, a summary expression, and the
contextual helpers. Here the summary is named after the caller's measure, so
`share_of_parent()` receives the same embraced name, and `grouping_bit()`
flags the rows that total the inner level:

```{r}
report_embraced <- function(data, outer, inner, by, measure) {
  data |>
    summarize_with_margins(
      {{ measure }} := sum({{ measure }}),
      share = share_of_parent({{ measure }}),
      inner_total = grouping_bit({{ inner }}),
      .by = {{ by }},
      .grouping = rollup({{ outer }}, {{ inner }}),
      .sort = "last"
    )
}

retail_sales |>
  filter(year == 2026L) |>
  report_embraced(region, store, year, revenue)
```

A whole Grouping specification is a value, so a caller can build one and pass
it as an argument, which `.grouping` takes as it stands:

```{r}
report_by_spec <- function(data, spec) {
  data |>
    summarize_with_margins(
      revenue = sum(.data$revenue),
      .by = "year",
      .grouping = spec,
      .sort = "last"
    )
}

store_hierarchy <- rollup(region, store)
report_by_spec(retail_sales, store_hierarchy) |>
  identical(direct)
```

`grouping_bit()`, `grouping_id()`, `share_of_parent()` and `share_of_total()`
read a bare name rather than a `.data[[ ]]` subscript; a name held as a string
reaches them as `!!rlang::sym(name)`. *Forwarding a column from your own
function* in
[`grouping_bit()`](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/grouping_bit.html#forwarding-a-column-from-your-own-function)
and *Forwarding a name from your own function* in
[`share_of_parent()`](https://sayuks.github.io/marginplyr/man/share_of_parent.html#forwarding-a-name-from-your-own-function)
say how a forwarded name is resolved.
